payload.claim: `survivor_claim_with_suite_verdict`'s guard `if result.verdict == "unproven" or result.uncounted: return claim` discards the kill even when `result.verdict == "killed"`, as long as `result.uncounted` is also non-empty. `check_probe` (saffron/probe.py:278-290) can return `verdict="killed"` with a non-empty `failures` tuple *and* a non-empty `uncounted` tuple at the same time (e.g. one new failure matches `counted` and a second new failure does not) — but the guard at line 791 fires on `result.uncounted` truthiness alone, before the `killed` branch at line 794 is ever reached, so the claim is returned unchanged (today's witness-only text) instead of naming the killing tests. This contradicts both the function's own docstring two lines above ("`killed` names every killing node id" — stated with no exception for coexisting uncounted failures) and the spec's settled rule (item 2: "A new failure among the head's collected tests is a kill") and `probe.py`'s own documented invariant that an uncounted failure "decides nothing" (saffron/probe.py:24-26) — it should not veto a kill that genuinely occurred. No test in this diff exercises a mixed killed+uncounted `ProbeResult`; the only uncounted-path test (`test_a_second_ask_whose_new_failure_no_head_test_names_keeps_todays_claim`) uses a pure `survived`+`uncounted` result, leaving this branch of the guard unverified.
